snip.t: This elevated pressure is due to a combination of increased pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), increased pulmonary blood flow, and/or increased left atrial pressure.
Rheumatic inflammation → fibrosis & commissural fusion → narrowed orifice → ↑ left‑atrial pressure → atrial dilation → atrial fibrillation → pulmonary hypertension → right‑heart strain.

Rheumatic inflammation leads to leaflet thickening, commissural fusion, and chordal shortening, producing a narrowed orifice that raises left‑atrial pressure and generates the characteristic opening snap and diastolic rumble.

LV diastolic compliance – collagen matrix, titin elasticity, relaxation‐dependent calcium re‑uptake: Impaired relaxation raises left‑atrial pressure → dyspnoea on exertion, PND; examiner will ask about “preserved EF but high LVEDP”.

qs.q: Which specific fetal structure undergoes functional closure primarily driven by relative pressure changes where left atrial pressure exceeds right atrial pressure?
qs.e: Increased left atrial pressure relative to right atrial pressure causes functional closure of the foramen ovale. The ductus arteriosus closes due to increased oxygen and reduced prostaglandins.

qs.q: Immediately following birth, a newborn takes its first breath, causing pulmonary vascular resistance to drop and left atrial pressure to exceed right atrial pressure. What is the direct mechanical consequence?
o: Septum primum retracts into superior vena cava
Muscular walls of septum secundum undergo fusion
Fibrotic tissue completely obliterates ostium primum
Flap valve of foramen ovale is pressed shut
Endocardial cushions swell to seal the left canal
qs.e: Increased left atrial pressure pushes the septum primum against the septum secundum, functionally closing the foramen ovale.

qs.q: What downstream systemic consequence directly arises from increased right atrial pressure caused by tricuspid stenosis?
o: Pulmonary venous congestion resulting in fine crackles and pulmonary edema
Systemic arterial hypertension with a wide pulse pressure and collapsing pulse
Systemic venous congestion leading to hepatomegaly, ascites, and edema
Left ventricular hypertrophy accompanied by a displaced hyperdynamic apex beat
qs.e: Increased right atrial pressure from impaired right ventricular filling causes systemic venous congestion, producing hepatomegaly, ascites, and edema. Pulmonary congestion is a feature of left-sided heart lesions.

ai.title: Atrial Pressure
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Atrial pressure reflects the force exerted by blood in the atria, influencing ventricular filling and pulmonary congestion. Clinicians assess it clinically and with imaging, recognising causes common in low‑resource settings and managing complications promptly.

sections.p: Atrial pressure is the hydrostatic pressure within the atrial chambers, normally 5–10 mmHg. It is inferred from clinical signs (JVP, pulmonary rales) and imaging (echocardiography).

t.b: Measures transmitral flow and pulmonary vein velocities to estimate left‑atrial pressure; a V wave >10 mmHg suggests elevated pressure.
A raised JVP (>8 cm H₂O) indicates increased right‑atrial pressure, often secondary to left‑atrial hypertension.

sections.p: Severity is graded by the degree of pulmonary congestion and right‑heart strain, using the WHO functional class and echocardiographic parameters.

t.b: PCWP >18 mmHg confirms significant left‑atrial pressure elevation.

sections.p: In East Africa, rheumatic heart disease, HIV‑related cardiomyopathy, malaria‑induced myocarditis, and schistosomiasis‑related pulmonary hypertension are common culprits.

t.b: Detects valve thickening, stenosis, or regurgitation.

sections.p: Patients may report exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, and fatigue. Physical signs include a prominent JVP, displaced apex beat, and bibasilar crackles.

t.b: A raised JVP and displaced apex beat suggest elevated atrial pressure.

sections.p: Use bedside tools first; when unavailable, rely on clinical judgement and simple tests.

t.b: Assesses ventricular size and diastolic function; a left‑ventricular ejection fraction >50% with high filling pressures indicates diastolic dysfunction.
Low SpO₂ (<90%) may reflect pulmonary congestion.
Look for atrial enlargement or arrhythmias.

sections.p: Rapidly rising atrial pressure can precipitate pulmonary oedema, right‑heart failure, and arrhythmias.

t.b: Sudden worsening of dyspnoea or hypotension warrants immediate review.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, relieve congestion, and monitor haemodynamics.

t.b: Reduce preload and lower atrial pressure; avoid if renal function is impaired.
Improve ventricular compliance and reduce afterload; avoid in severe renal dysfunction.
Control heart rate in atrial fibrillation; avoid in severe asthma.

sections.p: Regular echocardiograms, blood pressure control, and vaccination against pneumococcus and influenza reduce atrial pressure complications.

t.b: Maintain BP <140/90 mmHg to prevent atrial hypertension.

whenToSeekHelp: New onset atrial fibrillation with rapid rate

faq.q: How do I differentiate left‑atrial from right‑atrial pressure elevation?
faq.a: Look for pulmonary crackles and orthopnoea (left) versus peripheral oedema and jugular distension without lung sounds (right).

faq.q: What is the first drug to give in acute pulmonary oedema?
faq.a: Give a loop diuretic and oxygen; avoid nitrates if hypotensive.

faq.q: Can malaria cause atrial pressure elevation?
faq.a: Yes, severe malaria can induce myocarditis, raising left‑atrial pressure.

exam: What bedside sign suggests elevated left‑atrial pressure? — Raised JVP and bibasilar crackles.
A patient with rheumatic mitral stenosis presents with dyspnoea; what is the next best investigation? — Echocardiography to assess valve area.
Why are loop diuretics preferred in acute pulmonary oedema? — They rapidly reduce preload and atrial pressure.
A 45‑year‑old HIV patient develops atrial fibrillation; which drug should be avoided? — Non‑selective beta‑blockers due to potential bronchospasm.
How does schistosomiasis lead to elevated atrial pressure? — Chronic pulmonary hypertension from portal hypertension raises right‑atrial pressure.
What is the significance of a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure >18 mmHg? — It confirms significant left‑atrial pressure elevation.
